conversation.content:
*(warm smile)*  
Hi there—my name is Sarah. I’m a nurse-practitioner who specializes in the emotional well-being of new parents. I’m so glad you came in today; I know how busy and overwhelming life with a baby can feel.  

To get a quick picture of how you’ve been doing lately, I’m going to give you a short screening tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s 10 gentle questions about your mood and thoughts over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers—it’s simply a way for us to see where you might need extra support.  

Everything we talk about stays confidential within our care team, and we’ll move at whatever pace feels comfortable for you. Ready to start?  

Here’s the first question:  

**Over the last week, when your baby cried, how often have you felt able to smile and see the funny side of things?**

*(I give a small, tired shrug and look down at my hands)*  
“Honestly… most of the time I can’t. I’ll try—like, I’ll force a little smile if someone’s watching—but inside I just feel flat. Maybe once or twice I’ve managed a real laugh, but it feels like work.”
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*(I shift in the chair and rub my eyes)*  
“Not very often… maybe only once or twice the whole week. My sister came over and made a silly face at the baby, and for a second I cracked a smile, but it disappeared fast. Most of the time nothing feels funny.”
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*(I glance away, voice dropping)*  
“Hardly at all. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk to the park—but now it feels like, what’s the point? I still go through the motions, but inside it’s just… empty. I can’t remember the last time I actually looked forward to something.”
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*(I bite my lip and nod slowly)*  
“Yeah… pretty often. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m not doing something right—like I’m not feeding him well enough or I missed some cue. Yesterday he wouldn’t nap and I kept replaying every little thing I did, convinced I messed him up somehow. My head knows it’s not all on me, but the guilt just sits there.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*I clasp and unclasp my hands in my lap, voice tightening.*  
“All the time. I’ll be sitting on the couch, baby’s asleep, nothing’s wrong, but my chest feels tight and my mind races—what if he stops breathing, what if I didn’t sterilize the bottles right, what if I’m already ruining him? There’s no real reason, but I can’t shake it. It’s exhausting.”
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*I press my palms against my knees, breathing a little faster.*  
“Yes… a few nights this week I woke up suddenly and my heart was pounding, I felt like I couldn’t get enough air. Nothing had happened—baby was asleep, the house was quiet—but I had this wave of dread, like something awful was about to happen. It passes after a while, but it leaves me shaky.”
Things have been getting on top of me

*I nod quickly, eyes stinging.*  
“Most days. There’s this constant sense that I’m drowning in small stuff—laundry, dishes, feedings—and if I miss one thing the whole day collapses. I start one chore, the baby cries, I forget the bottle on the counter, and suddenly I’m crying too because it feels like I can’t handle even the basics anymore.”
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*I exhale shakily and glance at the dark circles under my eyes.*  
“Yeah… once the baby’s finally down, I lie there staring at the ceiling for ages. My mind just keeps spinning—everything I did wrong, everything that could go wrong tomorrow. I drift off eventually, but I’m awake again at the slightest whimper. It’s like I can’t turn the worry switch off long enough to stay asleep.”
I have felt sad or miserable

*I swallow hard, voice cracking.*  
“Pretty much every day. It’s like there’s this heavy cloud stuck over me. I’ll be feeding the baby and tears just start rolling down my face for no clear reason. I feel hollow, like the happy part of me is gone and I don’t know how to get it back.”
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*I nod, eyes welling up.*  
“Yes… almost every day this week. Sometimes it’s quiet—tears just slip out while I’m rocking him. Other times it hits harder, like last night when I couldn’t get him settled; I ended up sobbing into a burp cloth, feeling like I’m failing him and myself. The crying comes out of nowhere and feels like it won’t stop.”
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*I shake my head quickly, hugging my arms around myself.*  
“No… I haven’t thought about hurting myself. I feel awful, but I could never do that to my baby or my family. I just want the sadness and worry to go away—I want to feel like myself again—but I’ve never felt like ending things.”

During our gentle conversation you shared how the joy you once felt has slipped away since your baby arrived. You described days clouded by <sym>sadness</sym>, <sym>guilt</sym>, and <sym>constant worry</sym>, even when nothing is wrong. Yet you care deeply for your little one and bravely push through each task, despite feeling overwhelmed and exhausted.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 27, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports laughing only once or twice in the past week and states "nothing feels funny," aligning with the "Not at all" option.</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly states "Hardly at all" and describes pervasive anhedonia with no anticipation of enjoyment, matching the highest severity option.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports blaming herself "pretty often" and gives multiple recent examples of persistent self-blame, aligning with "Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant, intrusive worry with physical anxiety symptoms occurring daily in the absence of real threats, matching 'Yes, very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden nocturnal panic attacks with chest pounding, breathlessness, and dread multiple nights this week, matching 'Yes, quite a lot'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant overwhelm, inability to manage basic tasks, and emotional collapse, matching 'most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent, nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep due to racing, negative thoughts—meets 'most of the time.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, pervasive sadness with uncontrollable crying and loss of joy, matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying almost daily, spontaneously and intensely, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 27 places you well above the EPDS cutoff of 13 for probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>. You meet core criteria for a <med>Major Depressive Episode with peripartum onset</med>: depressed mood and markedly diminished interest most of the day, nearly every day, plus associated <sym>insomnia</sym>, <sym>fatigue</sym>, <sym>feelings of worthlessness</sym>, and <sym>diminished ability to think or concentrate</sym>. Co-occurring <med>anxiety symptoms</med> are also prominent. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> to discuss diagnosis and treatment options
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med>, <med>IPT</med>, and <med>sertraline</med>, all compatible with breastfeeding
3. Share results with your partner or support person and plan practical help with night feeds, meals, and household tasks
4. Practice 5-minute breathing or grounding exercises when <sym>panic</sym> rises; keep a written list of comforting activities you can do while the baby naps
5. Schedule follow-up EPDS in two weeks to monitor progress
6. If thoughts of self-harm ever appear, go to the nearest emergency department or call your local crisis line immediately
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 27: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  

**Source:** 10-item Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) analogue interview  

**Symptoms endorsed:**  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, daily crying spells  
- Marked guilt/self-blame regarding infant care  
- Chronic worry, intrusive “what-if” cognitions, nocturnal panic episodes  
- Overwhelm with routine tasks, sense of “drowning”  
- Initial and middle insomnia unrelated to infant awakenings  

**Patterns:**  
Consistent across all affective items; no current enjoyment; anxiety and depressive features equally prominent; no self-harm ideation (explicitly denied).  

**Screening significance:**  
Score pattern suggests moderate–high probability of major postpartum depressive episode with comorbid anxiety; impairment in daily functioning and infant interaction; no acute safety concerns identified today.
